1.grade_fit_note: Grade-6 word, but the context ("Show me. Then do it again.") nearly gives it away; sits at the easy edge of grade 6.
1.note: Key is clean and unique. 'Amazed' and 'impatient' are both reasonable traps, but the sister's demand for a repeat signals doubt clearly enough that the item plays easier than 190-199.

2.grade_fit_note: Paired commas around a nonrestrictive clause is core grade 6-7 punctuation.
2.note: Options form a balanced 2x2 (comma before 'which' yes/no x comma after 'flood' yes/no), so no option wins on majority features. A student who knows commas come in pairs cuts A and D, which is the skill being tested, not a free kill.

3.grade_fit_note: Correlative conjunctions are a named grade-5 standard (L.5.1e).
dimensions_varied: polarity/meaning of the pair (negative, alternative, additive)
whether the correlatives are correctly matched (D pairs neither with or)
3.note: B and C are ruled out by logic ('so the school rented a tent'), not grammar; only D tests correlative form. That works, but 'Neither' appears twice and 'nor' only once, so a test-wise student leaning on 'neither' has to tell A from D, which is the point of the item.

4.grade_fit_note: Cause-effect transition with a very clear relation (5 bags down to 2 after composting).
4.note: Unique key. The cause-effect link is explicit enough that this plays closer to grade 5 than grade 6. 'In addition' and 'Meanwhile' are live traps for weaker readers.

5.grade_fit_note: Direction versus region is in scope for grade 5, but it is the classic hard capitalization rule.
5.note: Balanced 2x2 (North/north x Midwest/midwest), no structural tell. Lowercase direction plus capitalized region trips many grade-5 students, so I would expect it to land a band above 180-189.

6.grade_fit_note: Shift in pronoun person/number (L.6.1c-d) is a grade-6 target.
6.note: 'your' is the real trap (a colloquial person shift) and 'their' is a decent one. 'his' only works if the student reads 'muscles' as the coach's, which hardly anyone will.

7.grade_fit_note: Tier-2 word with context giving one positive and one negative reason.
7.note: Clean. Each distractor matches one half of the passage (nervous or upset for leaving friends, excited for the studio), which is good distractor design.

8.grade_fit_note: 'Privilege' is a frequently misspelled grade 6-7 word.
8.note: Balanced 2x2 (privi-/prive- x with/without d), so no majority-feature tell. All three misspellings are real student errors.

9.grade_fit_note: Strong context ('tiny sips', 'plenty' at the start) suits grade 5.
9.note: 'leak out' is the main trap. 'taste stale' has no support and only a careless guesser would choose it; 'grow warm' is weak but conceivable.

10.grade_fit_note: Double consonants plus -ence/-ance is a demanding grade-7 spelling.
10.note: Balanced 2x2 (cc/c x -ence/-ance); every distractor is a common real misspelling. Good item.

11.grade_fit_note: Contrast with 'simple' plus a list of features is grade-5-friendly context.
11.note: 'handmade' is literally true of the card ('Priya made'), so a student matching facts rather than meaning could defend it, but the 'simple' contrast points to 'detailed'. Formatting defect: the passage text sits inside the Question field while the stem says 'as it is used in the passage'; move it to a Passage block to match the other vocabulary items.

12.grade_fit_note: Clause function (L.7.1a) is grade 7; noun clauses are at the hard end of that.
dimensions_varied: syntactic role (modifier of Room 12, object of knew, subject, adverbial of place)
12.note: D is a strong trap because 'where' invites 'tells where'. A (modifying Room 12, which sits inside a prepositional phrase) is implausible, and C fails because 'Nobody' is plainly the subject.

13.grade_fit_note: 'Necessary' is a standard grade 5-6 spelling demon.
13.note: Balanced 2x2 (c/cc x s/ss); no structural tell. Could play slightly harder because the word is so often misspelled.

14.grade_fit_note: Family titles after a possessive are grade-5 capitalization.
14.note: Balanced 2x2. 'my' governs both nouns, so both are lowercase. D is the best trap, since students learn to capitalize 'Grandma' when it is used as a name.

15.grade_fit_note: Choosing a precise word is a grade-7 skill, though the cue here is strong.
15.note: Sentence 4's exact '18 milliliters' rules out 'estimated' and the vaguer verbs. The cue is explicit enough that the item plays a band easier than 200-209.

16.grade_fit_note: Perfect tenses are a named grade-5 standard (L.5.1b-c).
16.note: Options are a clean tense x aspect 2x2. 'since ...' plus 'still runs' requires present perfect. D 'teaches' is the natural trap.

17.grade_fit_note: Intensive pronouns are a named grade-6 standard (L.6.1b).
17.note: Balanced 2x2; 'theirselves' is a common nonstandard form and a real trap. Most grade-6 native speakers will find it easy, so it may land at the low end of the band or just below it.

18.grade_fit_note: Contrast context plus a vivid example; fine for grade 6.
18.note: 'speedy' is the reversal trap (Owen's trait), and 'proud' and 'helpful' are loosely consistent with Grace. Clean key.

19.grade_fit_note: Introductory-element comma and series commas are grade-5 standards (L.5.2a-b).
19.note: Balanced 2x2. Some style guides allow dropping the comma after a short introductory clause (four words here), so A is defensible in adult usage. Under the grade-5 standard C is the key, but consider lengthening the opening clause to remove the argument.

20.note: Balanced 2x2 (comma in 'long, boring' x comma in 'new, winter'). It pairs a coordinate case with a cumulative one, which is the right test of the skill.

21.grade_fit_note: Grade-7 word, but 'repaired' and 'replace them' make the meaning easy to infer.
21.note: Unique key. 'get slippery' and 'dry out' could also justify closing a bridge, but 'replace' and 'not repaired for years' point to decay. The context is generous for 200-209.

22.grade_fit_note: Misplaced and dangling modifiers are L.7.1c.
dimensions_varied: position of the phrase (sentence start, after the object, sentence end, between verb and object)
noun the phrase sits next to (Marco, pizza, table, verb)
22.note: B is the classic dangling trap. C is technically misplaced (the phrase sits nearest 'table' and could attach to Marco), but readers resolve it to the pizza, so some will argue for it. D's split of verb and object is so awkward that few will choose it.

23.grade_fit_note: Language names versus general school subjects is grade 5-6 capitalization.
23.note: Balanced 2x2 (French/french x science/Science). B is the strongest trap, since students often capitalize every school subject.

24.grade_fit_note: Historical events versus century names is grade 7 capitalization.
24.note: Balanced 2x2. D (capitalizing 'Nineteenth Century') is the live trap, and lowercase 'civil war' will catch weaker students.
